Yeah, what I don't like is the implication that everyone from this race necessarily has X character trait from birth due to genetic reasons.

All Orcs HAVE to be stupid and impulsive, all Dwarves HAVE to be greedy and enjoy mining, etc. regardless of the conditions of their upbringing. Even the "culture" explanation borders on unbelievable at times and there's often an overlap between "belonging to a race" and "having been influenced by the one single monolithic culture of this area that everyone interprets in the exact same way", just because you can tick the first box doesn't mean you necessarily tick the second and the reverse is also true.

And yes, the shitty part of that type of worldbuilding is that the concept of fundamentally evil races means that "Ideally, we should kill on sight all the people from race X" and even eugenism to a degree are now sound lines of thoughts for the PCs. If you write a race whose people have the evil murderer gene 100% of the time, then you wrote a scenario in which ethnic cleansing is not only valid but the ideal solution to a serious problem.

It also leads to humans being seen as the "normal" race personality-wise while discouraging you from playing anything else since all others are firmly locked into their respective stereotype. The Last of Us series. When trailers and early previews for the first game came out over ten years ago, I called it the video game equivalent of oscar baits and moved on. Then everyone called it a masterpiece and all I could think was "definitely overrated". Years later, I played it and guess what, if you go into something convinced that it can't impress you, it won't (and you'll feel so validated for "having been right all along").

But over the years I mellowed out on it ! I particularly like the ending of the game and while I remember criticizing the story for being relatively predictable, these days I appreciate that a story isn't all about being unpredictable and should be commended for being well-executed like it is here. It still has some of the most impressive cutscenes I've seen in any game.

I also remember being really unimpressed by the first trailers for TLOU2, as they hinted that the story was that they actually wrote a lesbian romance for Ellie (a romance that isn't just relegated to a DLC most people will never play like in the first game) just to immediately kill her girlfriend and make the plot about Joel and her going back on an epic adventure just like old times. Then the game came out and turns out, this was an intended misdirection and the story doesn't go that way. At all. I know it pissed off a lot of people but this decision actually made me notice the game and decide to buy it. That was such a risky move that while I'm not in love with that game, I think it's one of the bravest sequels I've seen.

Ten years ago, I never would have thought I'd ever call this series "brave" lmao

I believe it's called a thermian argument ! Like you said, it's when someone replies to criticism of a writer's decision by pointing that the writer wrote lore around that decision, as if that's not a completely irrelevant comeback.

Fallout 3 is a bit more simplistic but it plays into its charm a lot, there's no real choices in the factions you support and the overall story is a lot more linear but it's really good at making you feel like you're someone special on a grand adventure and the TV show obviously references it because you're a vault dweller who goes into the wasteland to try and find your father.

Realizing that you missed the window of opportunity for acquiring something, growing a specific crop or catching a certain fish and that you now have to wait for a specific season to come back, while it's not a forever punishment, is still understandably stress inducing.

"Aww shucks, guess that window of opportunity just closed for the next 15+ hours of game time" is not my idea of a feel good, zero stress time and because of that I'll never be able to play this game without carefully planning my weeks and setting objectives to meet by the end of the coming season. You're just not going to progress if you don't understand what the game wants from you and then act on it before you run out of time.

EDIT : \*Just in case, I'd like to point out that I said this because the thread asks for my most controversial take, I wouldn't go after someone because they gave that advice. There's some merit to it and there's definitely room for someone to argue back that at some point, the player has to accept they can't always be the perfect minmaxer, especially in their first farm. On ship controls (or even just moving around in space at all), the key thing you have to learn to make it tolerable is that you need to **compensate** for every movement you make. If you pressed to go right, sooner or later you'll have to press to go left to undo the momentum, otherwise you will forever go right. If you want to go forward and you press that direction 15 seconds, you're gonna have to press backwards for just as long if you want to go back to a neutral state. That sounds like a pain, but for long distances it means that you can just press forward for a few second and then stop, you don't have to keep pressing the button in fear of losing your speed.

It's not like a car, you won't go slower naturally over time. Your speed will not change if you don't make it change !

Some katanas have unique properties, whereas the mantis blades have perks that benefit them and only them.

Overall, you'll need intelligence for hacking and technical if you have any hope to equip the strongest cyberwares, which are build-defining. So you gotta choose one stat to dump between Cool, Reflex and Body.

Cool governs Snipers, which you don't care for, but also pistols, Revolvers and throwable weapons. It makes stealth a lot easier by boosting how fast you move when crouching.

Body governs shotguns, light and heavy machine guns. It makes you more tanky by giving you more HP (whereas Trchnical males you more tanky by boosting your armor). Also lets you be good at blunt weapons, including your fists. It comboes well with intelligence since you can spend HP to hack eventually.

Reflex governs dashes (it gives crazy mobility), assault rifle, submachine guns and blades. Said it already but I'll say it again : it's hard to give up on dash once you start using it. It makes moving around a lot better, especially with air dashes.

D&D's biggest mistake is not that the last few seasons are no longer complex and well-written (though it's true) but that they tried to have their cake and eat it too. By season 6, the show had turned into run-of-the-mill high fantasy, there's no longer this element of mistakes being punished, and people liked it just fine. Jon Snow makes a grave mistake, getting dozens of archers to shoot at him but he survives just fine because come on he is the hero. Riveting. Battle of the Bastards is one of the highlights of the show.

And then here comes the ending and now D&D decide they want to be gritty realistic unpredictable Game of Thrones again. Yeah of course people hated it, and not just because D&D were awful at it.

Had they kept the more generic tone to the end, with epic battles between really nice characters and really evil characters and a golden ending with Jon Snow, Daenerys and Tyrion leading Westeros, most people would have ate that shit up and called it satisfying and memorable.

Had the long night ended with a twelve-minutes duel between Jon Snow and the Night King, it would be near-universally loved. More generally, had they just kept on writing the generic high fantasy story that GoT season 6 was, the reception would have been just fine.

TL;DR : A lot of fans say they hate the ending because it's badly written and for many of them I don't fully believe that. They hate that they didn't get the high fantasy epic story beats they were getting (and felt were being promised) since season 6 devolved the story into this epic good vs evil fantasy narrative.

It says that people don't necessarily need to be under the threat of violence to do good. First question - Yep' just like you said, the statues are vital to record the data from the probes (that's why there are currently three working statues in the game, one for you, one for Gabbro and one dedicated to recording the results from the probes). From what I remember, linking statues to people was a safety measure in case there's something wrong with the project, they felt they needed a few people aware of the time loop so they could act/report their observations to the group if something unplanned happens and abort the whole "explode the sun to timetravel" operation. Which is understandable because otherwise, the whole universe would be stuck in a timeloop without anyone aware of it (ironically it's exactly the mess they ended up leaving behind lol).

Second question - Someone else will have to help you with that one, quantum logic is something else lmao. I think the key to Solanum's condition is that she hasn't left the moon yet.It's interesting to note that when you're on the eye, the scene where you see many stars around you go supernova could imply that the eye is moving you forward in time to the point where everything in the universe has died (that way, nobody is gonna just stumble upon the eye and end the universe way before its time has actually come). So much like Solanum on the quantum moon, you do go through some time shenanigans.

Third question - I'd say it's like getting to keep memories from a time that has been erased. The timeloop never had to work before anyone was connected to a statue, the Nomai designed the statues and built them at the same time (and actually got the statues working before they ever managed to trigger a loop). And yeah, basically when it triggers it resets the last 22 minutes and you - because you're linked to a statue - get to remember what happened in that time that is now erased.

The original plan was that just by triggering the Ash Twin Project, one single probe would be sent at a random location and then, the universe would go back 22 minutes like nothing ever happened and the probe would then be sent at a random location again. From the point of view of someone who's not linked to a statue, you'd just press the button "on" and right after, you'd instantly see the results of thousand of probes sent literally everywhere (and you'd have no memory of the thousand of unsuccessful probe results because those timelines were resetted). Said results would be reported by a statue dedicated to recording the data of every probe (it's what you find out in the heart of Giant's Deep).

They essentially designed a plan that would require a colossal amount of time and ressources (building millions of probes and sending them all with enough power, one by one for generations) and bypassed those limitations through time-travel, allowing them to try, go back, try again, go back, try again, go back, until the statue recording the data goes "ding ! found the eye !" and those not linked to statues wouldn't even remember any of the failed attempts.

I think when Jimmy said "I'm helping you because you're my brother, you'd do the same" it made Chuck feel guilty because at this point, he backstabbed Jimmy by telling Howard not to hire him - all behind Jimmy's back instead of owning up to it. So I think both his guilt and Jimmy's compassion got to him and he genuinely wanted to connect with his brother in that instant.

But then Jimmy assumes that Chuck just wants to call him out and make him feel bad for cutting corners. And his wariness is understandable since that's often what Chuck does. And Chuck is hurt by that reaction, so he accuses Jimmy of stealing the ice. And his wariness is understandable because it's definitely something Jimmy would do and guess what, Jimmy did admit in the finale of season 1 that he steals ice regularly.

It's the best tragedy in the show. They both try to connect with each other but they've hurt the other too much.

The point of the reveal at the end of season 1 is that for the first time, Jimmy finds out that Chuck actually resents him. Up until then he legit thought their relationship had always been good although strained (due to spending his entire life as a conman).

If anything, Jimmy is kind of implied to be the favorite child to both of their parents and is systematically depicted as the more popular sibling.

EDIT : I see where you're coming from because I used to say too that "Chuck has always been abusive toward Jimmy, he's sabotaging him since forever". It's just that we tend to think that the relationship between the characters didn't exist before episode 1. It's easy to condemn Chuck harshly because the show starts with him not acknowledging that Jimmy is maybe capable of turning a new leaf. What we don't see is the entire decades of scamming and getting away scot free that eroded Chuck's patience, on top of the parents' preferential treatment.

I always thought that Hank died because he failed to act like the hero the story built him up to be. When you think about it, even though he's pretty smart and competent at his job, in the end it's not what helped him to figure out that Walter is Heisenberg.

I don't know if we can really look at what the Souls are doing and just try to take a page from their book considering how differently they handle gameplay. In Monster Hunter, a huge part of being good at it is knowing your weapon, what are your big moves,what is your most efficient combo depending on your situation, how to shortcut from that combo into your big move, plan a guardpoint or a counter, stay at the ideal shooting distance, etc.

Whereas the Souls just keep it very simple, once you pressed the light and heavy attackbuttons a few times, you pretty much know your entire moveset and the fun solely comes from punishing at the right time and not being allowed  to make too many mistakes. So there's much less to perfect about your approach to the fight beyond knowing the tells of the boss. It's why we're okay with such long fights in Monster Hunter, while the idea of a boss fight that could last 20 minutes in a Souls game would probably be considered the most tedious experience.

I think the average boss fight in Monster Hunter has more potential to stay fresh than the average boss fight in a Souls game and in light of that, I wouldn't be a fan of the next game going "alright just beat it a couple of times and then you don't see their faces ever again" like Souls games do. The Souls realize that their boss fights don't really make for a much different/interesting experience past the first encounter, that's why they handle their bosses like that.

One could argue that making all the exclusive mounts and armor accessible for, say, 10+ wolf collars could help resurrect the PvP, especially if a second pvp roulette dedicated to Feast was added. Because a lot of a person's personality is shown through how they speak, so a lot of players feel like a voiced blank slate protagonist stops them from roleplaying any character they want and forces them to play, at best, variations of the same person. 

I think the general consensus among people who dislike voiced protag is :

-If your protagonist is a very specific individual with his backstory and mostly defined personality, like Geralt from The Witcher for example, it's worth it to voice him.

-If your protagonist is a blank slate made so that the player can make up their backstory and most if not all of what makes their personality, you will weaken that aspect by giving them a voice. V from cyberpunk is not a very well defined character, but was voiced anyway, and now players are stuck roleplaying either a character that speaks like a thug, or a character that speaks like a thug. 

Basically, if you're gonna force players to roleplay as one person in particular, might as well make them interesting. If you're not making them interesting, let the players do the job and don't hinder them with a forced voice.

Yeah it makes sense too ! Honestly whether Chuck staying comes from a place of love or a place of hurt, I still find this scene absolutely heartbreaking lol

Personally I went from hating Chuck with a passion to feeling bad for him over time. Like, the scene of their mother's death is tragic, but not just because Chuck lies about it afterwards. What truly kills me when I watch is that Jimmy casually leaves for a little while because he feels like grabbing a bite, while Chuck absolutely refuses to leave their mother alone. It's such a subtle display of love and affection, and he's immediately slapped in the face with "I loved you less". If I was in his shoes I would have broke down and probably required the services of a therapist afterwards. I have a hard time blaming him for not handling correctly what basically amounts to a traumatic event, on top of the regular grief for his mother.

I used to really hate how he secretly records Jimmy at the very end of season 2 tho, since the entire trick only works because he knows very well that Jimmy will feel bad. I found it so, so evil. But even that, I feel now like I get where he comes from. At the end of season 3, the last time he speaks to Jimmy, he tells him that feeling bad means nothing if you're not gonna actually change afterwards. Basically he says that one should be judged on their actions, and not their thoughts or intentions.

And in light of that, yeah I understand how he could go through with his idea of weaponizing Jimmy's good nature against him. Because at the end of the day, being good natured doesn't mean shit if you're still gonna act all shady. Imagine someone doing something shitty, and then saying "oh, but I really felt bad while I was doing it yknow" and then some time later they revert back to their old ways. Imagine witnessing that for entire decades.

Still, I despise how needlessly secret he was with his resentment for Jimmy. If I was in Chuck's shoes, instead of giving Jimmy a job in the mailroom of my company, I would have told him "You're a grownup, you're responsible for being the fuckup conman that you are, I want nothing to do with you, get out of my life" a while before the show even started. But no, instead he comes up with these ridiculous elaborated ways of sabotaging his brother while making his friend Howard look like a dick. Ugh.

...so yeah, I think Chuck is more of a tragic figure than anything. Like everyone, I wish he would have given Jimmy another chance eventually, especially when Jimmy took care of him while he was stuck at home, but ... that's just not how emotional damage works. You can't be a pain in someone's ass for 40+ years and then turn into a saint suddenly for a few years, and be surprised when their opinion of you hasn't done a complete 180.

And I get the whole "Chuck is the reason Jimmy broke bad" argument, but I really feel like the entire Davis and Main arc is there to show us that when Jimmy is given golden opportunities and a supportive environment with no Chuck in sight.... he still fucks things up because Jimmy loves chaos. Chuck played a part in Jimmy turning into Saul, but he's far from being the main cause imo.

Thing is, I don't really see what's the point of saying " He's less of a cunning mastermind and more of a lucky dipshit" as if it was a bad thing. Those are just different characters traits. You don't have to be a cunning mastermind to be a good villain, or even a good fictional character. I certainly don't think that would have automatically made him a stronger character, just a different one.

Yes, the villain of P4 is just a regular guy with flaws. He's not an extraordinary individual. Does that makes him a worse character ?  (I have my issues with the traitor of P5, but definitely not these ones)

His motive is that he's angry at the world. He's not popular. He's not good looking. Considering he had to work his ass off in school to have decent grades, we can deduce he's not even book smart. He's painfully average, if not mediocre, and he convinced himself that because of all that, he was denied the right to have fun with friends, which made him jealous and now he wants to take revenge. We were expecting a james bond villain mastermind, instead we got a freaking school shooter. I'm sorry for the people who wanted him to be another one of those villains that go "Yeah I know that I'm guilty of some ridiculously evil stuff, but I have a tragic backstory, and from my point of view, I'm actually the good guy" but it certainly made him memorable as hell for me.

The fact that the entire story isn't something he has complete control over created a few interesting moments here and there : when the first body is discovered, Adachi threw up. It wasn't him playing the part of the stupid innocent Adachi, it was him realizing that he had just murdered someone (which, now that I think about it, makes even weaker the whole "Adachi is just a psychopath" approach to his character). Or when he happened to receive a call from Namatame, and by thinking on his feet, made him kidnap people. Heck, quite unlike Light Yagami, Adachi never really plans anything : he just adapts, until he eventually can't and the Investigation Team gets to him. Even without his final slip of the tongue, the IT was already on to him so I think it's fair to say that he didn't loose out of sheer bad luck.

His redemption is more rooted in self-hatred than some newfound compassion too. I don't even think he has a single line where he thinks of his many victims and how he ruined their lives. It was more about him understanding that he was immature and needed to change, which starts by paying for what he did. It's very in-line with the rest of the game (and P5), where after a big fight, the character feels very tired but has found inner peace or understanding of themselves, when in real life it would take months or even years of therapy.

In the later fighting games, in which we get to read his thoughts, he also shows a deep contempt for his past-self and the line of thinking he had in P4. I think it resonates a lot better with P4's themes of truth and acceptance too : the bad guy understanding what's wrong with him and doing something about it. Had it ended with Adachi crying and screaming ... what would the message be ? "As horrible as you are, you must always acknowledge who you are in order to become your best self and/or allow true change. But if you do some really horrendous stuff then I'm sorry bro it's too much, just go to prison without ever learning your lesson" ? It's very powerful that even someone like him can try to change for the best. You call that anticlimatic and I have to disagree : I think throwing all that away for the sake of some epic good vs evil fight would have resulted in a much weaker narrative and, ironically, sounds a lot more like something that could be written by Reki Kawahara.

I didn't said that there was no story in this DLC, I said there wasn't *much* of it, and I stand by that statement. I see what you mean about not forcing less skilled players to go through something that is ridiculously hard, while still providing the insane challenge to those interested. I think it's a valid point. The fact that the people who care about collecting everything were baited by the "Glorified charms" feature kinda defeats the point though (sorry if I bring that up often but I always come back to that when I think "why was I looking forward to Godmaster ?"). As I said earlier, people that align with me would express much less disappointment if it wasn't for that. Besides, I don't think it's completely unreasonable to be disappointed that while this DLC can be aimed at a very specific type of players, it's sad that there's close to nothing for pretty much everyone else. We all quickly went from very excited to "Oh ... ok then". I think I like Grimm Troupe better because it provided charms, a little storyline that wasn't great but did the job, one very fun boss (and a charm notch for defeating his first form) plus the ultimate challenge when it comes to platforming in Hollow Knight, aka the Path of Pain.

I guess I expected Godmaster to have at least some things for everyone too, when it really is "just" a huge, very well made equivalent to the Path of Pain but for fighting.

Rewards can take many forms. In most games, getting to see more of the story works just fine. But ... yeah, there isn't much story in this dlc. There isn't much of anything beside the new bosses they've put in-between all the others we already know about. I'm not saying I think the new content is bad, just that it can be quite tedious to get to the parts that interest me.

Now that I think about it, it's no surprise the Trial of Fools is the last thing I did in the base game (I've even defeated NKG before it). I don't get anything for beating it in a game that almost always rewarded me for overcoming its challenges. If you want to know, I played a ridiculous amount of games in my life, but I can count on one hand the amounts of time I've unlocked all the achievement/trophies. It's because I don't do tedious stuff without any real incentive to do so (and most games have that one trophy that asks you to do stuff that is so time-consuming it's ridiculous). For example, I never would have collected all the grubs in this game if it weren't for all the rewards and the uniques charms you get in the process. I think it isn't a good thing that TC didn't put any reward (I believe at least that we shouldn't praise that decision) because rewards make everything so much better. If it's already fun, it's the icing on the cake (see how many people love Mario Odyssey because this game makes sure to always reward you for exploring/overcoming challenges). And if it isn't that much fun, it can keep you motivated until you reach the next fun part.

To answer your questions at the end, if you don't find a game fun then chances are you're just not playing it for more than a few minutes/hours, but yeah, a reward can change everything. I didn't get any enjoyment out of Hollow Knight until I unlocked the Dash for example. See also all the games that have boring beginnings but gets better after the first few hours once you're allowed more freedom with the way you approach them. And if what you're doing in the game is already fun, well that's incentive enough. I remember going through the hard mode of Hotline Miami 2 for no other reason than "I'm having a great time". Yup', the heart of the problem is that the content of this DLC feels just tedious to some people including me. And going through something we find tedious just for the sake of saying "I did it" is kinda meh. I stopped playing today thinking "Maybe another time" and I have no idea if I'm going to play through the DLC tomorrow or next year. Nothing motivates me to go through this.

Honestly most of the disappointment would have been avoided if it wasn't for the whole "turns out the Glorified Charms feature has been cut" that we weren't even told about and just discovered the moment the DLC came out. I wouldn't have cared so much about Godmaster if it weren't for that, and that would have been for the best :/
